questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Negation of "Paris is in France and London is in England" is
options: Paris is in England and London is in France.
Paris is not in France or London is not in England.
Paris is in England or London is in France.
questions.solution:
Let $p$ : Paris is in France.
$q$ : London is in England.
$\therefore$ We have, $p \wedge q$
Its negation is $\sim(p \wedge q)=\sim p \vee \sim q$
ie, Paris is not in France or London is not in England.

questions.solution:
Inverse of $p \Rightarrow q$ is $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q\therefore$ Inverse of $(p \wedge \sim q) \Rightarrow r$ is
$\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \Rightarrow \sim r$
i. e., $\quad(\sim p \vee q) \Rightarrow \sim r$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If every element of a group $G$ is its own inverse, then $G$ is
questions.solution:
Let $a$ and $b$ be any element of group $G$.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore  a=a^{-1}, b \geq b^{-1}, \forall a, b \in G \\
& \text { Now, }(a b)^{-1}=a b[\because a, b \in G \Rightarrow a b \in G] \\
& \Rightarrow  b^{-1} a^{-1}=a b \Rightarrow b a=a b \forall a, b \in G
\end{aligned}$
Hence, commutative law holds in group $G$.
Therefore, $G$ is abelian group.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The negation of the compound proposition $p \vee(\sim p \vee q)$ is
questions.solution:
The negation of the compound proposition \(p \wedge(\sim p \vee q)\) is,
\(\begin{aligned}
& \equiv \sim(p \wedge(\sim p \vee q)) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim(\sim p \vee q) \\
& \equiv \sim p \vee(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv(p \wedge \sim q) \vee \sim p
\end{aligned}\)

questions.q: The proposition $(p \rightarrow \sim p) \wedge(\sim p \rightarrow p)$ is
questions.solution:
The truth table of $(p \rightarrow \sim p) \wedge(\sim p \rightarrow p)$ is as follows:
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\hline \boldsymbol{p} & \sim \boldsymbol{p} & \boldsymbol{p} \rightarrow \sim \boldsymbol{p} & \sim \boldsymbol{p} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{p} & \begin{array}{c}
(P \rightarrow \sim P) \wedge \\
(\sim p \rightarrow p)
\end{array} \\
\hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{~F} & \mathrm{~F} & \mathrm{~T} & \mathrm{~F} \\
\hline \mathrm{~F} & \mathrm{~T} & \mathrm{~F} & \mathrm{~F} & \mathrm{~F} \\
\hline
\end{array}$
Clearly, last column of the above truth table contains F only. So, the given statement is a contradiction.
